rationale: The roster forces editorial_macro, and it genuinely fits: this story turns on one physical thing — the fuel port each house already has — and what that thing costs. A macro diptych states the $686-versus-$2,977 split through material contrast alone: calm brass on clean drywall against rusted steel and amber oil, with no numbers needed.
cue: the fuel the house already burns
subject: a split-pair of residential fuel ports — a clean brass gas shutoff valve on a copper line versus a rust-streaked galvanised heating-oil tank's fill pipe and amber sight gauge in a basement
core_thesis: NEADA's November 10 forecast prices the same winter four ways — $686 flat for a natural-gas household, $2,977 up 70.2 percent for a heating-oil household — because the fuel already plumbed into the house, not anything bought this month, sets the bill.
core_conflict: Flat, domestically priced natural gas versus heating oil tied to global diesel markets through the Strait of Hormuz — one winter, two fuels, season bills sitting 4.3 times apart.
composition: Split-screen diptych with a clean vertical seam: left half the pristine gas valve on bone-white drywall, right half the rusted oil tank and amber sight gauge; hero details sit on the thirds with generous negative space under one raking light.
